opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, the core idea is that mathematics is the language underneath almost all of science, and right now it's also one of the biggest bottlenecks. A physicist or a biologist will often have an intuition, a conjecture, a model they believe is true, and then getting from that intuition to a rigorous result can take months or years, or simply never happen because the right expert isn't in the room.

What we want to build at Axiom is an AI mathematician that can actually reason, not just produce text that looks like math. That's why we care so much about formal verification, about systems like Lean. If the AI proposes a proof, we want it checked line by line by a machine, so a scientist doesn't have to wonder whether it's hallucinating. Being verifiable is what makes it something you can trust and build on.

I see it supporting research at a few levels. First, as a collaborator for mathematicians themselves: exploring many approaches in parallel, filling in the tedious lemmas, finding counterexamples quickly, so humans can spend their energy on the creative, conceptual parts. Second, as a bridge for other sciences. A lot of fields are bottlenecked by optimization, by proving properties of algorithms, by checking that a model's assumptions are consistent. An AI that can formalize and verify those pieces lowers the barrier enormously. Third, there's a longer-term picture where the AI is generating its own conjectures, its own problems, and discovering structure we haven't noticed, almost like a self-improving loop between conjecturing and proving.

And I think it changes who gets to do mathematics. When I was a student, so much depended on whether you had access to the right mentor or community. If a curious high school student or a researcher in a smaller institution can work alongside a reliable AI mathematician, that's a real democratization of rigorous thinking.

So the hope isn't to replace mathematicians. It's to give human curiosity a much more powerful and much more trustworthy instrument, kind of like what the telescope did for astronomy.

r002.rationale: It describes an AI mathematician as a bridge for other sciences that can formalize and verify theoretical work, giving researchers a reliable collaborator for mathematically rigorous questions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The way I think about it is that mathematics is the language that almost every quantitative science is written in, and right now the bottleneck in a lot of fields isn't data or compute, it's the mathematical reasoning that turns an idea into something rigorous and usable.

So the first thing I hope Axiom's AI mathematicians do is take the long, grinding parts of that process off the researcher's plate. If you're a physicist or an engineer or a biologist and you have a conjecture, you shouldn't have to spend six months finding a collaborator who can check whether it's actually true, or whether there's a counterexample sitting right there. An AI mathematician that can formally verify a proof, or tell you precisely where it breaks, compresses that cycle from months to hours. And because the output is a formal proof rather than a plausible-sounding argument, you can actually trust it. That's the part I care about most. We're not trying to build something that sounds like a mathematician, we're trying to build something whose work holds up under the same scrutiny we'd apply to a human proof.

The second thing is exploration. A lot of discovery in science is pattern recognition across areas that don't usually talk to each other. A technique from algebraic geometry turns out to crack a problem in optimization, or something from combinatorics ends up being exactly what a cryptographer needed. Humans are limited by what they've personally read. A system that has internalized the whole literature and can search over it with real rigor can surface those connections, propose candidate lemmas, and let the human scientist spend their time on the judgment calls, which is where people are genuinely irreplaceable.

And then, longer term, I think of it as expanding the frontier itself. There are open problems in math that, if they fell, would immediately unlock things in materials science, in cryptography, in the foundations of machine learning. I don't think an AI mathematician replaces the human mathematician. I think it's closer to giving every researcher a tireless, honest collaborator who never gets bored of the hard parts, and who will tell you when you're wrong. If we do it right, the effect isn't that there's less mathematics being done by people. It's that there's far more mathematics being done, in far more fields, by people who previously couldn't afford to do it.

astra-6.text:
My hope is that AI mathematicians can become collaborators for scientists—helping them formulate questions precisely, explore conjectures, and check whether an argument really holds up. A scientist might have an intuition about a system but need new mathematics to understand it. We’d like to make that mathematical work more accessible, so they can move between intuition and rigorous reasoning more easily.

What excites me most is the possibility of discovering something together that neither the researcher nor the AI would have found alone. That requires more than producing an answer: it requires reasoning that people can inspect, verify, and build on.

sol-6.1.text: My hope is that AI mathematicians can become collaborators for scientists—helping them explore conjectures, work through difficult derivations, and check whether an argument really holds up. Mathematics underpins so much of scientific research, and a mathematical bottleneck can slow down an entire project. If we can help researchers move through those bottlenecks with reliable reasoning, they can spend more time asking new questions and understanding what their results mean. Ultimately, I’d love to see these systems help people discover things they wouldn’t have found on their own.
